answer.sourceLine: The line closes a paragraph in “A Bad Trip,” which first ran as a Notes of a Dirty Old Man column in the underground paper Open City for 27 September–3 October 1967. It was collected by City Lights in Erections, Ejaculations, Exhibitions, and General Tales of Ordinary Madness (1972) at p. 440, and reprinted in Tales of Ordinary Madness (1983) at p. 200.

source.excerpt: I have met free men in the strangest of places and at ALL ages — as janitors, car thieves, car washers, and some free women too — mostly as nurses or waitresses, and at ALL ages. the free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it — basically because you feel good, very good, when you are near or with them.
trail: The Bukowski Database records the piece first running as a Notes of a Dirty Old Man column in Open City ↗, dated 27 September–3 October 1967, opening with Bukowski’s line about LSD and colour television arriving for consumption at the same moment.
The same database files the collected version under the title “A Bad Trip” ↗ and gives its book placements: p. 440 of the 1972 City Lights omnibus and p. 200 of Tales of Ordinary Madness.
Wikipedia confirms the publishing chain: the 1972 City Lights volume ↗ was republished in 1983 as two books, and Tales of Ordinary Madness lists “A Bad Trip” in its contents ↗.
Wikiquote carries the sentence under its Tales of ordinary madness heading ↗ — but with no page reference, which is the sourceless form nearly every quote site has copied.
source.excerptNote: Bukowski wrote his Open City columns in trademark all-lowercase, so the sentence begins “the free soul,” not “The free soul.” The capitalised version that circulates online is a later tidy-up.
source.rightsHolder: The Estate of Charles Bukowski; City Lights Books
source.rightsNote: This is not a public-domain text. The column dates to 1967 and the book that first collected it, Erections, Ejaculations, Exhibitions, and General Tales of Ordinary Madness, was published by City Lights in 1972 ↗ — comfortably inside US copyright, as is the 1983 Tales of Ordinary Madness reprint. The short passage above is quoted for identification and comment.

author.name: Charles Bukowski
author.heading: Charles Bukowski
author.metaLine: 1920–1994 · Los Angeles poet, novelist & underground columnist
author.bio: Born Heinrich Karl Bukowski in Andernach, Germany, on 16 August 1920 and raised in Los Angeles, he spent years in low-wage work and the US Post Office before Black Sparrow Press publisher John Martin put him on a stipend in 1969 so he could write full time. From 1967 he produced Notes of a Dirty Old Man, a column for the underground paper Open City — the source of most of the prose City Lights later gathered into Erections, Ejaculations, Exhibitions, and General Tales of Ordinary Madness. He died in San Pedro, Los Angeles, on 9 March 1994.

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: The words really are Bukowski’s. What gets mangled is where they came from, how they are worded, and what they are about.

items.why: Quote sites circulate only “The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it.” ↗ — dropping the clause that carries the whole idea, and capitalising a sentence Bukowski wrote in lowercase.

items.who: “Tales of Ordinary Madness” on its own
items.why: Goodreads credits only the 1983 selection ↗. That book is a repackaging: the essay is a 1967 newspaper column, first collected in 1972.
A second Goodreads entry files the same line under Bukowski’s German birth name ↗, with no source, as though a different writer had said it.

Pinned over sunsets and couples, it reads as a love line. In the essay it sits inside an argument that most people are conditioned into obedience by the age of seven or eight — a piece about acid, television and conformity ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuine Bukowski, correctly placed: the sentence ends a paragraph in “A Bad Trip,” his Open City column of 27 September–3 October 1967, collected at p. 440 of the 1972 City Lights volume — per the Bukowski Database record ↗.

context.heading: An acid essay, not a love letter
lead: “A Bad Trip” opens with Bukowski noticing that LSD and colour television reached American living rooms at roughly the same moment, and that the country outlawed one and ruined the other. The argument that follows is about conditioning: bad trips, he claims, are mostly caused by people who were trained and frightened into shape long before they ever swallowed anything — most of them captured, he writes, by the age of seven or eight. The hippie slogan about not trusting anyone over thirty gets no mercy either; thirty, he says, means nothing.

The famous sentence arrives as the exception to that gloom. Free people exist, he insists, and he has met them in unglamorous places — janitors, car thieves, car washers, nurses, waitresses — at every age. The test he offers is not a description but a sensation: you identify a free soul by how you feel standing next to one. Read in place, it is a line about escaping social training, not about falling in love.
detailsBody: Bukowski’s Open City columns were set in lowercase throughout, which is why the authentic sentence begins “the free soul is rare.” Almost every version online silently capitalises it, and many also swap his dash for a comma or a full stop.

The 1972 City Lights omnibus was later split in two: half became Tales of Ordinary Madness and half became The Most Beautiful Woman in Town, both in 1983. That is why the same line is variously credited to a 1972 book and a 1983 one. Both credits are right; neither is the first appearance.
context.pull: You identify a free soul by how you feel standing next to one.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Bukowski Database records the story "A Bad Trip" as dating from 1967 and lists its book appearances as Tales of Ordinary Madness (1983), pg. 200 and Erections, Ejaculations and General Tales of Ordinary Madness (1972), pg. 440; it also links an alternate version titled "Notes of a Dirty Old Man".

The Bukowski Database entry for the alternate version carries the same opening text ("did you ever consider that lsd and color tv arrived for our consumption about the same time?") as a 1967 story appearing in the magazine Open City, September 27–October 3 1967.

Wikiquote's Charles Bukowski page lists "The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it - basically because you feel good, very good, when you are near or with them." under the heading "Tales of ordinary madness (1967-83)", with no page citation attached to that bullet.

Tales of Ordinary Madness was first published in 1983 by City Lights Books, culled from the 1972 paperback volume Erections, Ejaculations, Exhibitions, and General Tales of Ordinary Madness, and its contents include "A Bad Trip".

Erections, Ejaculations, Exhibitions, and General Tales of Ordinary Madness was published by City Lights in 1972 and was republished in two volumes in 1983 as Tales of Ordinary Madness and The Most Beautiful Woman in Town.

Charles Bukowski was born Heinrich Karl Bukowski on 16 August 1920 in Andernach, died 9 March 1994 in San Pedro, Los Angeles, wrote the column "Notes of a Dirty Old Man" for the underground publication Open City beginning in 1967, and left the postal service in 1969 after Black Sparrow Press publisher John Martin offered him financial support.

A reproduction of the essay "A Bad Trip" contains the sentence in its original lowercase form, immediately preceded by "I have met free men in the strangest of places and at ALL ages – as janitors, car thieves, car washers, and some free women too – mostly as nurses or waitresses, and at ALL ages.", inside a passage arguing that most beings are captured and trained by the age of 7 or 8.
Goodreads carries the quote in lowercase form credited to Charles Bukowski with the source given as Tales of Ordinary Madness.
Goodreads carries a duplicate of the same quote credited to "Heinrich Karl Bukowski." with no book source given.
Quotefancy circulates the truncated, capitalised form "The free soul is rare, but you know it when you see it." credited to Charles Bukowski with no book source.

BookRags' study-guide entry for the chapter "A Bad Trip" in Tales of Ordinary Madness describes it as Bukowski on acid and colour television arriving together and on a society whose citizens are anesthetized, dulled and conditioned; it does not quote the "free soul" sentence.
